title: Transactions are Generally Available, advancing warehousing on the Lakehouse
abstract: Multi-Statement Transactions are Generally Available , enabling organizations to run complex, multi-step workflows with atomic guarantees without needing separate warehouse systems. Data warehouses power some of an enterprise’s most important workloads, including data ingestion, transformation, business intelligence, applications, and operational analytics. Many of these workloads require changes across multiple tables to succeed or fail together. Historically, organizations relied on separate warehouse systems for these transactional guarantees, adding expensive data movement, duplicate copies, fragmented governance, and operational complexity. Databricks is the first lakehouse architecture to support multi-statement transactions natively across both Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables. Alongside stored procedures, temporary tables, and SQL scripting, multi-statement transactions bring traditional data warehousing workloads to open, governed data on the lakehouse. Traditional and cloud warehouses provide transactional guarantees, but often at the cost of a fragmented data architecture: Multi-statement transactions bring these guarantees directly to the open, governed lakehouse, reducing duplicate systems and the operational work required to keep them aligned. Transactions on the lakehouse provide a foundation for running demanding warehouse workloads on open enterprise data. They combine support for open table formats with unified governance and high-concurrency performance. They also integrate with familiar warehouse development tools, data pipelines, and production observability capabilities. Open across Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg Multi-statement transactions support both Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables. Teams can preserve open table formats while gaining atomic guarantees across multiple statements and tables. They do not have to move governed data into a proprietary format or maintain a transactional copy in another system. The lakehouse architecture supports row-level concurrency, allowing concurrent transactions to write to the same table as long as they do not update the same row. Unlike traditional data warehouses, which use locks to serialize writes, row-level concurrency enables more transactions to run in parallel. As a result, Databricks delivers significantly stronger performance than traditional cloud and legacy warehouses, allowing organizations to run demanding warehouse workloads directly on the lakehouse. Integrated with warehouse development and data pipelines Transactions are composable with other warehousing capabilities, enabling teams to build traditional data warehousing workloads on the lakehouse. For example, developers can stage intermediate results in a temporary table , package multi-step business logic in a stored procedure , and commit the entire workflow atomically. Transactions can also write to streaming tables , bringing atomic guarantees to workflows that continuously ingest, transform, and publish data. Now, downstream pipelines can receive consistent updates, preventing them from processing incomplete data. Governed transactions on sensitive data Transactions respect Unity Catalog attribute-based access controls, including row-level security and column masking, on both reads and writes. This is especially important for workflows that stage, validate, and publish sensitive data. Observability in in production Production transactions need to be understandable as well as correct. Developers can use commands such as DESCRIBE TABLE , SHOW COLUMNS , and GET DIAGNOSTICS to inspect the tables involved in a transaction and capture information about transactional execution. These capabilities make transactional workflows easier to develop, operate, and troubleshoot. This fully integrated experience enables Fivetran to build their connectors on top of lakehouse transactions. Likewise, Accolade uses transactions to process thousands of claims and liabilities records every day. Together, open formats, centralized governance, row-level concurrency, familiar SQL features, pipeline integration, and observability create a complete transactional experience on the lakehouse. Multi-statement, multi-table transactions support several common patterns for modernizing ETL, migrating warehouse workloads, and publishing trusted data. Give ETL multi-table transactional guarantees An ETL job can update related tables as one unit. In this example, the order status and inventory balance cannot fall out of sync. If either update fails, the workflow can roll back both changes rather than publishing a fulfilled order without the corresponding inventory adjustment. Migrate warehouse procedures to the lakehouse Stored procedures and temporary tables let developers preserve familiar warehouse development patterns while operating on governed lakehouse data. Unity Catalog row-level security and column masking policies continue to apply to governed reads and writes. The procedure also uses DESCRIBE TABLE to inspect the target’s schema and metadata before the next set of writes, helping developers verify its configuration and troubleshoot issues without leaving the transactional workflow. Write-Audit-Publish prevents data from becoming visible until it passes the required quality checks. The workflow stages new data, records its quality results, and publishes the validated records in one atomic operation. If a validation or write fails, the transaction can roll back instead of exposing a partial result. The same pattern can include transactional writes to streaming tables when downstream pipelines need the published data continuously. Multi-Statement Transactions are Generally Available for UC managed Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables on Databricks. Get started with transactions today using Databricks’s documentation or by prompting the in-product Assistant. With transactions on the lakehouse, you can bring critical warehouse workloads to open, governed data while reducing duplicate systems, data movement, and operational complexity. title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
abstract: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”

title: “thegentlemanpervert” producing AI CSAM is a NJ prosecutor, say cops
abstract: New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on “felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” Bucks County Detectives said in a press release Thursday. In the US, cops have vowed to crack down on AI CSAM since at least 2024, when the Department of Justice made one of the earliest arrests . After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.” New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested at his home Thursday. Credit: via Bucks County Detectives New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested at his home Thursday. Credit: via Bucks County Detectives On Thursday, New Jersey officials accused 51-year-old Fitzgerald of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media. Fitzgerald was charged after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received a tip that a Discord user shared an illicit image in July. Cops then used “digital forensics and subscriber records” linked to the Discord account and “associated Internet protocol addresses” to track the user to Fitzgerald’s home address. After a search Thursday, cops “recovered prompts and scripts used to create artificially generated child sexual abuse material using an AI program,” the press release said. They also found Discord chat logs where Fitzgerald, under the Discord username “thegentlemanpervert_2160_07833,” allegedly “admitted to making multiple illicit images using artificial intelligence and sharing them with other users.”

title: Leaked Anthropic Draft AI Regulatory Bill Is Unacceptable and Troubling
abstract: There is a newly leaked bill that Anthropic is purportedly shopping around is (if you assume its bugs get fixed). It is similar to the FRONTIER Act, with stronger preemption of state laws, stronger transparency provisions and weaker enforcement provisions. Having slept on this, I find it unacceptable that Anthropic is actively shopping exactly the type of bill I have warned we will need to fight against during the lame duck session. They are trying to use this last time with a Republican Congress to pass preemption of exactly the important state laws, and get some transparency but not much enforcement in exchange. This reads as intentional, that Anthropic is more afraid that the government might enforce rules against Anthropic, than they are worried about the ability of the government to enforce rules against everyone. Anthropic’s policy team seems to have, chosen protecting their business interests and guarding against their political risk, at the expense of safety considerations. There was no need for the company purportedly existing to promote safety to propose a bill that is not even actively stronger than the FRONTIER Act, when the FRONTIER Act was a compromise bill proposed back in June. Even if you were fine with what is being given up, what you get in return very obviously does not meet the moment. Nor is there any need for such compromises. It seems rather insane for Anthropic to be proposing it now. This seems like the bill that someone on the anti-regulatory side should be pushing. It is not obvious this makes us safer than doing nothing, even if the alternative is fully nothing at all levels. Say it isn’t so, Anthropic, or at least that it was a mistake and is no longer so, or I am going to be rather cross. I am at a conference and cannot do an RTFB, but it feels important to get word of this out quickly, especially so Anthropic employees can look into this and ask questions. If you want the full text, here is a copy . I have not had the time to do so, but the other usual suspects quickly sprinted to RTFB (read the bill) and they did not like what they saw. You can try to call this a ‘pretty reasonable AI safety bill’ as Charlie Bullock does, but that is by the standards of people trying to protect the industry from more impactful regulation. POLITICO : Anthropic quietly pitches its own AI safety bill to lawmakers . Ketan Ramakrishnan : Anthropic’s new federal AI bill is, without any overstatement, astonishingly bad. Charlie Bullock : Big news. My take: Anthropic deserves some credit for actually proposing a pretty reasonable AI safety bill; that’s more than other frontier labs have done. But they don’t deserve *too* much credit, IMO; this bill is weaker than the Trahan-Obernolte FRONTIER Act in some key ways, and since the political momentum has shifted significantly in the direction of safety since FRONTIER was introduced back in July, I think new bills introduced today should ideally go further than FRONTIER was able to go rather than regressing. To be fair to Anthropic, the main places where this bill is significantly weaker than FRONTIER are (a) rulemaking (very strong in FRONTIER, almost nonexistent in Anthropic’s bill) and (b) the emergency shutdown authority. Even if you take safety seriously, it might make some sense to dial those authorities back if you didn’t trust the executive branch to wield them responsibly, because those are the easiest provisions for a hypothetical President who hypothetically might not like a certain frontier AI company to abuse. There are some improvements over FRONTIER as well; for instance, this bill does specify that auditors are employed on a continuing basis and has better provisions regarding auditor access to information. Happy to see that from Anthropic (although I think their access provision is still a little undercooked and has Fourth Amendment problems). Overall, I think the embedded auditor bills that get introduced in the coming months are going to be significantly better and more ambitious than this, and I hope Anthropic supports those bills instead of opposing anything that treats catastrophic risks like the serious national security issue they are. Still, it’s encouraging to see a frontier lab come this far. Charlie Bullock : I think the drafting is okay. I’ve seen better but I’ve definitely seen worse. Claude is a pretty good legislative drafter. There are a few clear mistakes but that’s par for the course in a leaked discussion draft. Nathan Calvin : Charlie’s analysis is right but he is nicer than I am – I found myself viscerally angry at multiple points reading this bill. There are some good and sensible parts, but overall this legislation is not remotely close to meeting the moment and I overall think passing it would make us less protected against catastrophic risks than we are under existing law. Two parts that stand out as particularly infuriating when taken together: 1. Some of the preemption provisions are remarkably far reaching and consequential, and in addition to preempting legislation like SB 53 would also remove general powers that state courts have to enjoin defendants and protect the public. Most outrageously, it has a provision that looks like its intended to stops states from enforcing laws or judicial decrees that “suspend the development, deployment, or internal use of an AI model” to protect their citizens from imminent catastrophic harms. Such powers to block and suspend model deployments would then only reside with the federal government. 2. The federal governments powers to restrict the development, deployment, or internal use of a frontier model has to meet an absurdly high bar. First, there needs to be an imminent risk of a catastrophic harm (meaning killing more than 50 people or causing more than a billion dollars in damage). But thats not enough! The agency head needs to make a detailed determination with no deference given to show why no alternative would prevent the imminent catastrophe. Next the court is also explicitly told to consider the harms to the developer and other harms from restricting the model, but no considerations in the other direction. This is absurd! For all of its warning about the potential for AI to cause a catastrophe that kills literally everyone on the planet, Anthropic’s proposed federal law likely makes it harder than under existing law for a court to get an order blocking or restricting the development of frontier models? WTF?? There are also a bunch of others things that I would like to see improved – the substantive details of the auditing section and the potential for rule-making on substantive safety standards both come to mind – but I think these stand out as particularly indefensible. Charlie Bullock : Nathan’s righteous anger has inspired me to make one more mildly disapproving observation: it’s kind of wild that the Anthropic bill has no government licensing for the independent auditors. Licensing is, IMO, the bare minimum thing that you need to even be able to pretend that your auditing regime isn’t just going to devolve into a race to the bottom. Without it, auditors will inevitably compete with each other to offer their customers, the labs, the least bothersome audits available at the lowest possible price point. Obviously Anthropic trusts itself to do a great job of picking great auditors, but do they trust OpenAI to do the same? What about SpaceXSI? The new Anthropic bill is weaker than their June framework, and offers both forward-looking and backward-looking preemption in exchange, despite months of movement to enable us to do more. What are we even doing? Nate Soares : Anthropic’s proposed law would make it even harder than it already is for a court to block or restrict the development of an AI that threatens all humanity. Alex Bores : Anthropic is pitching a bill that closely matches its framework from June.

title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
abstract: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I’ve sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here’s what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the “Start new voice chat” button—that’s not the microphone button, it’s the one to the right of it—and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it’s a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here’s an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it’s not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don’t want it on the tag pages. I don’t want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they’re... published, like once they’re made public a month after they’ve gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist . We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I’d have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR . I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page , or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter . The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages. GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen. OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay —and they do work well in that environment. I don’t think this is going to be a daily driver for me though. I’ve written before about how much “work” I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog—mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code. This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn’t work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent. I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words. I mainly work from home, which is good because there’s no way I’d want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace! The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead. This is A new feature for my blog, built using my voice by Simon Willison, posted on 9th October 2026 . title: [AINews] High Taste Testers Ep. 1
abstract: We are piloting a new show on Latent Space: High Taste Testers, a variant of our food show where we pull you in to a typical lunch conversation in San Francisco. All your favorite talking points, starting with Dev Day and going into the latest models and assistants, are here: AI News for 10/15/2026-10/16/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! US Open-Weights Push: Muse Spark Open and Reflection Beam Muse Spark Open (Meta) : An 816B-total, 42B-active MoE with open weights. Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 ( AA ). Architecture and footprint : 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Pricing and efficiency : Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models ( cost ). Vals counts 55.5M output tokens across its index, the fewest of any open model, but says input tokens drive most of its cost ( Vals ). Weak spot : It ranks last among the top nine open models on AA’s four agentic evals while leading open models on AA-Omniscience. Vals places it #12 among open-weight models and #38 overall ( Vals ). Arena ranks it the top US open model on Code Arena WebDev with 1511 points, #13 among open models ( Arena ). License : The custom Muse Model License requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution. Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue need a separate agreement with Meta. Ecosystem : mlx-lm had day-0 support with vision, plus an Apple blog post on RDMA-distributed inference across Mac Studios ( @zcbenz ). vLLM served RL rollouts during Muse training and supports the release at launch ( vLLM ). SemiAnalysis has added B200 configurations to InferenceX ( SemiAnalysis ). Criticism (opinion) : @teortaxesTex calls it “DOA” against the smaller, MIT-licensed V4.1 Flash. He also speculates, without evidence, that Meta withheld Spark 1.3 because of distillation from OpenAI ( speculation ). @alexandr_wang describes MSL as having built “a machine that builds new models.” Reflection Beam 1.0 : A 501B-total, 23B-active MoE with 1M context, released under Apache 2.0. The release includes BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 weights, a DFlash2 drafter, the open Mirror CLI harness Beam was trained on, and a safety report ( Reflection , safety report , Mirror ). Independent evals : AA scores it 30, #2 among US open models, using about 26k tokens per task. It reaches 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA but only 3.0% on Terminal-Bench 4.0. On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% correctly but hallucinates at 47% ( AA ). Arena places it #12 among open models in Agent Arena (±3.84%) and makes it the only non-Chinese model in the top 25 open models on Code WebDev ( Arena ). Architecture : Sliding-window attention with a 512 window in a 5:1 pattern, no RoPE, Llama-4-style global attention scaling, gated attention, QK-norm, sandwich norm, logit softcapping and no shared experts ( @eliebakouch ). Serving and RL : vLLM had day-0 support. On 4× B300 with NVFP4 at TP4, it measured 1,769 output tok/s at concurrency 16. SkyRL offers day-0 LoRA, full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL, and reports +62% LoRA decode throughput (276→447 tok/s/GPU), which is a decode result, not an end-to-end training speedup ( vLLM , SkyRL ). Ollama is serving it free for a limited time, US-hosted with zero data retention ( Ollama ). Other open releases : StepFun released Step 5 Preview open weights ( Together ). Tencent shipped Hy Memory 2.0 and claims Hy-Memory-30B-A3B beats Opus 5 on memory frameworks ( Tencent ). Datalab released Indra, a 1M-parameter OCR model it says runs 15× faster than Tesseract on CPU ( @VikParuchuri ). Frontier Model Rollouts and the Decision-Model Category Gemini 4 Argon : Now available to Pro subscribers and in AI Studio Build ( @_philschmid , AI Studio ). Specs and pricing : The wide release raises the output limit to 1M tokens from 64K, sharing the window with input. Intro pricing is $2/$10 until Nov 30 ( DeepLearning.AI ). Results : Perplexity reports a new SOTA on its WANDR research benchmark ( @AravSrinivas ). Argon ranks #5 in Agent Arena at +13.2% ( Arena ). @MParakhin gives early praise for its math, with the caveat that it needs higher reasoning effort. Anthropic speed and price moves : Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10/$0.50 for prompts up to 100K tokens, about 90% cheaper than Haiku 4.5. It scores 39.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at max effort, versus 16.4% for GPT-6 Luna ( DL Weekly ). An Opus 5.5 fast mode at 2.5× speed is reported ( @kimmonismus ). Claude Code now gzips the conversation payload on every turn to cut latency ( ClaudeDevs ). OpenAI product updates : GPT-6 Astra Pro in ChatGPT now runs multiple agents on parts of a task in parallel, with faster responses and better tool use ( OpenAI ). GPT Live 1.1 improves multilingual voice, and nine new presets were recorded with native-speaking actors ( @reach_vb , OpenAIDevs ). Codex is believed to have one or two new models coming; this is unconfirmed speculation ( @kimmonismus ). Elorian Glimpse : A visual-thinking VLM that runs recurrent computation over latent visual states instead of text-only chain of thought. Claimed results : Elorian says it matches or beats Astra on 5 of 12 benchmarks at 17× lower token prices, trained on “hundreds of GPUs” ( @dustinvtran ). Informal test : @omarsar0 found 8 of 10 game boards fully correct, versus 5 of 10 for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Decision models (calibrated one-pass classifiers) : Liquid d1-ultra : Tops AA’s Decision Index at 65, ahead of Jev 1.14 at 57. Its non-hallucination rate rises to 85% from 2% for d1, but accuracy falls to 32% from 41%. Time per task is 92ms and price is $0.042 per M input tokens, with output free ( AA ). Perplexity pplx-decider v1.2 : Open weights in a 27B model at 2¢/M and a 4B Flash model at 1¢/M. The update adds reranking, single-pass multi-question inference that is up to 5× faster, and -latest slugs ( @AravSrinivas , @denisyarats ). Usage : OpenAI’s Live API added a Decisions API for fast tool delegation ( @juberti ). In one experiment, swapping Jev into Recursive Language Model sub-calls was half the cost and 6× faster than Haiku 5.5 on OOLONG at 1M tokens ( @Jnatanh ). Inference Hardware and Serving Systems TPUv7 on AgentX : SemiAnalysis reports 1.42× better perf per dollar than GB300 NVL72 FP4, calculated on an external, non-Google cost basis, and 2.5× versus MI355X ( SemiAnalysis ). Interactivity split : TPUv7 is up to 3.16× better than disaggregated GB200 at medium to high interactivity. GB200 FP4 keeps a 1.2× edge at low interactivity ( thread ). The run was served with vLLM through TorchTPU. Vera Rubin NVL72 on AA-AgentPerf : Up to 5.7× GB300’s throughput per MW on DeepSeek V4 Pro, falling to 2.8× on Kimi K3, with the largest gains at high per-user speed ( AA ). Peak throughput : The gap narrows to 1.14–1.45×. Vera Rubin also posts a record 906 tok/s per user on V4.1 Flash. NVIDIA submitted all of these results. AMD MI355X : 8× MI355X delivers 24.4% more throughput than HGX B300 on Kimi K3 at 50 tok/s per user, and 87.4% more tokens per dollar ( vLLM ). Inferact announced a collaboration with AMD to publish open per-model recipes for agentic serving ( Inferact ).

A wave of excellent AI Agent harnesses has emerged in recent years, each with its own focus: Claude Code / Cursor / Trae Solo brought model reasoning deep into the programming IDE; Claude Cowork introduced the notion of project-level isolation to desktop-side knowledge work; WorkBuddy connected agents to IM ecosystems such as WeCom and Feishu so AI is one message away. When we shift the lens from "one-shot programming" or "immediate Q&A" to long-running, multi-project productivity work , however, several questions remain open: When many projects run in parallel, can memory be white-box and traceable ? When the AI gets something wrong, can you pinpoint which memory entry caused it and edit it directly — without starting a new chat from scratch? Can token cost be tracked per task , so that running agents in the background actually becomes economically viable? Can tasks of different difficulty automatically be matched to different models , instead of burning the flagship model on trivial calls? When you step away from the keyboard, can the work keep moving? Can the agent proactively discover what's worth doing, report progress, and land results as files on disk ? PilotDeck is an incremental exploration around exactly these questions. It uses the WorkSpace as the fundamental unit — completely isolating files, memory and skills per project — and pairs it with three pillar capabilities: White-box Memory , Smart Routing and Always-on . The entire system natively supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and behaves consistently across front-ends (Web / CLI / IM). ✨ Key Highlights WorkSpace-Level Isolation & Accretion Every project gets its own file system, memory store and skill set. Parallel work no longer interferes with itself, retrieval has a bounded scope, and skills accrete naturally as each task grows — no more global context pollution. Traceable White-box Memory Memory generation, extraction, storage and retrieval are visible end-to-end. When the AI mis-remembers, you can pinpoint and fix the offending entry. Built-in Dream Mode consolidates memory in idle windows, and supports one-click rollback. Smart Routing & Cost Optimization Task difficulty is auto-detected; complex calls go to flagship models (e.g. Claude 3.5 Sonnet / GPT-4o), simple ones drop to lighter models. Through on-device / cloud co-orchestration and precise matching, token spend shrinks dramatically without sacrificing quality. Always-on Background Execution PilotDeck breaks the "you ask, it answers" loop: after you sign off, the agent keeps discovering candidate tasks, running long-horizon monitors, and finally lands deliverables as local files with a summary report waiting for you. 📊 Real-world Numbers The three pillar capabilities have shown clear advantages in production-grade workflows: 1. Smart Routing — ~70% cost savings on social-media workloads In Xiaohongshu-style social-media operations, enabling Smart Routing automatically demotes simple polishing / layout tasks to a sub-agent (e.g. Sonnet 4.5) and only invokes Opus 4.5 at planning checkpoints: Setup Model configuration Cost Multiplier Smart Routing ON Opus 4.5 (main) + Sonnet 4.5 (sub) $2.83 1.1× Smart Routing OFF All Opus 4.5 (main + sub) $12.58 5.0× Monolithic Single Opus 4.5 long-react (estimated) $12.20 4.8× 2. Smart Routing — 1/6 the cost while beating frontier models on hard tasks The research team benchmarked 7 complex tasks (multilingual podcast push, multi-source data reports, domain-specific literature review, codebase architecture docs, etc.). The "strong main + light sub" routing setup matches or beats the frontier single-model setup at a fraction of the cost: Setting Score Cost MiniMax-M2.7 single-agent 37.1 $1.90 Claude Sonnet 4.6 single-agent 69.1 $18.36 Sonnet 4.6 (main) + MiniMax-M2.7 (sub) 70.6 $3.15 3. White-box Memory — layout & tone never bleed across projects In black-box agents, mixing tasks in a shared context pool inevitably pollutes memory. PilotDeck's WorkSpace-scoped white-box memory addresses this end-to-end: Dimension Current AI Agents (black-box) PilotDeck (white-box) Visibility You can't see what the AI remembers, only what it outputs View every memory entry: what was stored, when, and which WorkSpace Control Once written, memory can't be edited or removed Edit / delete entries, pin critical decisions so they don't drift Traceability When it goes wrong, you can't find the root cause Generation → extraction → storage → retrieval, all auditable Isolation One shared pool — projects bleed into each other Scoped per WorkSpace; A's memory never reaches B Reversible After compression, the original is gone Dream-mode supports one-click rollback to the prior state 🖥️ UI & Demo PilotDeck ships an out-of-the-box Web UI with full WorkSpace management, white-box memory editing, and visualization of multi-agent collaboration. Use Cases All demos below are generated entirely by edge-side models via PilotDeck's Smart Routing — no cloud-side frontier model required. Work Document Generation "Survey the Chinese LLM application market and turn it into a formal HTML white paper." Process Result Mini-Game Development "Walk me through building an iOS AR mini-game Ball Finder in Vibe Coding mode." Process Result AI Engineering Platform Development "Build a low-code embedding fine-tuning platform from scratch." Process Result Audio-Video Editing & Social Media Operations "Push this English podcast to a global audience in Chinese / Japanese / French / Korean / Spanish / Arabic." Process Result (with audio) podcast_result.mp4 📦 Installation & Quick Start We provide one-line installers for macOS / Linux and Windows PowerShell, plus a source-based workflow for developers. Option A: One-line install (recommended, macOS / Linux) curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenBMB/PilotDeck/main/install.sh | bash The script checks/uses the supported Node.js 22 runtime (22.13+ and <23, required for the built-in SQLite runtime), clones the repo, installs dependencies, and builds the frontend. On Linux it can install missing system packages when sudo and a supported package manager are available. On macOS, make sure Xcode Command Line Tools and a Python with distutils are usable before running the installer. Once it finishes: If Node.js or npm package downloads are slow or unreliable on your network, set reachable mirrors before running the installer: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenBMB/PilotDeck/main/install.sh | \
  PILOTDECK_NODE_DIST_MIRROR=https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/node \
  NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY=https://registry.npmmirror.com bash You can also keep the official Node.js host as the primary source and opt in to one or more trusted fallback mirrors with PILOTDECK_NODE_DIST_FALLBACK_MIRRORS .

title: awslabs/aidlc-workflows
abstract:
AI-DLC - one core, many harnesses AI-DLC (AI-Driven Development Life Cycle) turns AI coding assistants into
structured, verifiable software-delivery workflows. One harness-neutral core
runs natively in Claude Code, Kiro CLI, Kiro IDE, Codex CLI, Cursor, opencode,
and GitHub Copilot. The Quick Start below installs the latest stable AI-DLC release. Quick Start 1. Install AI-DLC macOS, Linux, or WSL: curl -fsSL https://github.com/awslabs/aidlc-workflows/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh Windows PowerShell: irm https: // github.com / awslabs / aidlc - workflows / releases / latest / download / install.ps1 | iex The installer sets up everything AI-DLC needs: the native aidlc command and
every harness runtime. You do not need to install Bun or Node.js; a native
install runs its hooks and commands through aidlc and does not call bun .
On Windows, it installs for the current account
and automatically registers the bin directory in User PATH. Run it from a normal
PowerShell window; one opened with "Run as administrator" gets a warning and a
prompt, since installing as administrator is less safe. Open a new terminal
if another session cannot find aidlc . To skip both persistent and
current-process PATH changes, use -NoModifyPath .
Windows uninstall removes only the User PATH entry recorded as installer-owned.
On macOS, Linux, or WSL, follow the installer's PATH instruction if needed. Prefer to manage the project files yourself, or cannot install a native
executable? The manual-copy path is the one place Bun is needed: install Bun , download aidlc-copy-runtime-X.Y.Z.tar.gz from the release , and copy
the complete runtime/<harness>/ directory into your project. This path does
not require the native aidlc command. 2. Configure a project From the project root, select the harness you use: cd /path/to/your-project
aidlc config --harness claude
aidlc doctor Replace claude with kiro , kiro-ide , codex , cursor , opencode , or copilot . Running aidlc config without --harness starts the interactive
setup when a terminal is available. If you use Kiro IDE's own terminal in a
project folder you have not trusted yet, Kiro first asks whether you trust it.
Choose Trust Folder & Continue only for your own project or one you have
checked, because trusting lets the folder's .kiro hooks run commands on your
machine; otherwise choose Cancel and review the folder first (see First run ). 3. Start a workflow Open your harness in the configured project and describe the work: /aidlc Build a REST API for inventory management Codex CLI uses $aidlc instead of /aidlc . In Kiro IDE, first choose aidlc in the chat panel's agent picker. AI-DLC selects a workflow from the request,
asks for missing decisions, and stops at approval gates before moving forward. For provider setup, trust prompts, and harness-specific prerequisites, use the
guide in the table below. The complete walkthrough is in Getting Started . Pick your harness Harness Configure Open Invoke Guide Claude Code aidlc config --harness claude claude /aidlc Getting Started Kiro: Kiro IDE >= 1.1.70 / Kiro CLI >= 2.24.1 (v3) aidlc config --harness kiro-ide Open the project in Kiro IDE and choose aidlc in the chat panel's agent picker, or run kiro-cli /aidlc Kiro IDE Kiro CLI (V2) >= 2.6 aidlc config --harness kiro kiro-cli chat /aidlc Kiro CLI Codex CLI >= 0.145.0 aidlc config --harness codex codex $aidlc Codex CLI Cursor aidlc config --harness cursor Open Cursor or run agent /aidlc Cursor opencode >= 1.17 aidlc config --harness opencode opencode /aidlc opencode GitHub Copilot CLI >= 1.0.74 / VS Code >= 1.130 aidlc config --harness copilot Copilot CLI or VS Code /aidlc GitHub Copilot Model-provider setup belongs to the harness. Shipped project configuration
keeps the provider and model already selected by the user. aidlc config providers can apply Amazon Bedrock settings on supported project surfaces or
record manual setup for other harnesses. Kiro CLI and Kiro IDE need no provider
answer because model access comes with Kiro. For Kiro's v3 engine on Kiro CLI
2.24.1 or later, use kiro-ide , which pins it; kiro is Kiro CLI (V2)
( Kiro CLI says how an existing kiro project switches). The methodology itself is
provider-independent. Recommended Model AI-DLC works best with capable reasoning models. The current recommended model
is Claude Opus 4.8. If Opus is not available to you, or you are not sure where
to set the model and effort on your harness, see Choosing a Model and Effort . Why AI-DLC Ad-hoc AI coding loses context as projects grow. AI-DLC keeps requirements,
decisions, implementation, tests, and operational work connected through one
audited lifecycle: 5 phases and 33 stages from initialization through operation 14 agents: 11 domain experts, 2 reviewers, and an adaptive composer 11 workflow profiles for features, bug fixes, infrastructure, security,
proofs of concept, enterprise delivery, and other common work Human approval gates and source-bound review evidence 119-event audit trail plus persistent state, team knowledge, and learned rules The same deterministic engine across every supported harness Start with Workflow Profiles to compare
Classic, Express, and the focused workflows. See the AI-DLC Workflows 2.0 Specification for the architecture and methodology. Important Generative AI can make mistakes. Review generated output and costs before
acting on them. See the AWS Responsible AI Policy . Documentation Guide Use it when Getting Started Installing, configuring, and running your first workflow User Guide Using workflows, profiles, agents, knowledge, and approval gates Harness guides Handling provider, trust, and runtime differences Install and Lifecycle Updating, pinning, installing offline, using mirrors, or uninstalling Harness Engineer Guide Reshaping stages, agents, rules, sensors, and knowledge Development and Releases Taking a PR through AI review, preview testing, and stable publication Developer Reference Changing the engine, hooks, packaging, or tests Repository Layout core/ - hand-authored, harness-neutral methodology and engine core/tools/ - 94 aidlc-*.ts engine and authoring tools harness/<name>/ - thin, harness-specific manifests and integrations plugins/<name>/ - optional AIDLC plugins scripts/ - packaging, binary, installer, and release tooling tests/ - smoke, unit, integration, and end-to-end tests docs/ - user, harness-engineering, and developer documentation dist/ and dist-release/ - generated, ignored local outputs Edit core/ or harness/<name>/ , never generated dist* output. Development Install dependencies and generate every harness: bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun scripts/package.ts Useful commands: bun scripts/package.ts < name > # generate one harness bun scripts/package.ts --check # determinism guard bun tests/run-tests.ts --ci # smoke, unit, and integration bun tests/run-tests.ts --release # full release acceptance See the Contributing Guide for the complete
development workflow and Porting to a New Harness to add another runtime. Troubleshooting Run aidlc doctor from the project root first. Common fixes: Symptom Fix aidlc is not found On Windows, quit and reopen the terminal app or IDE (a new tab inside one that was open during the install keeps the old PATH), or use the direct command printed with -NoModifyPath . On Unix, apply the installer's PATH instruction. Project/runtime version skew Finish the active workflow, then run aidlc config Codex hooks do not run Trust the project hooks as described in the Codex guide Bedrock access fails Enable the configured models and verify AWS credentials and region Plugin stages disappear after refresh Run /aidlc plugin sync Refreshed skills do not take effect Start a new harness session See Troubleshooting for diagnostic and
recovery procedures. References AWS AI-DLC blog post AI-DLC Method Definition Paper Roadmap License

title: cline/cline
abstract:
Cline The open source coding agent in your IDE, terminal, & desktop. Docs Discord r/cline Feature Requests Join us! CLI Run Cline in your terminal.
Interactive chat or fully headless
for CI/CD and scripting. npm i -g cline Learn more Desktop App Cline as a native app for macOS and Windows.
Run agent sessions in any folder, schedule
routines, and manage models, plugins, and MCP servers. Download for macOS and Windows VS Code Extension AI coding assistant in your editor.
Create files, run commands, browse the web,
and use tools with human-in-the-loop approval. Install from VS Marketplace JetBrains Plugin The same Cline experience in IntelliJ IDEA,
PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, and the rest of
the JetBrains family. Install from JetBrains Marketplace SDK Build your own AI agents and integrations powered by the same engine that runs the CLI, desktop app, VS Code extension, and JetBrains plugin. Custom tools, multi-agent teams, connectors, scheduled automations, and more. npm install @cline/sdk Documentation Index Product Description Location CHANGELOG SDK Node.js programmatic agent API and extension exports. sdk/ CHANGELOG.md CLI Terminal UI, headless mode, shell commands, and CLI-specific flows. apps/cli/ CHANGELOG.md VS Code Extension The Marketplace extension and extension host integration. / (WIP migrating) CHANGELOG.md Desktop App Native macOS and Windows app (Tauri shell, Bun sidecar, Next.js UI). apps/examples/desktop-app/ CHANGELOG.md JetBrains Plugin JetBrains-hosted client that talks to the shared agent core. Currently we are not open-sourcing JetBrains plugins - Docs site Public documentation pages. docs/ - Edits Code Across Your Project Cline reads your project structure, understands the relationships between files, and makes coordinated changes across your codebase. It monitors linter and compiler errors as it works, fixing issues like missing imports, type mismatches, and syntax errors before you even see them. In VS Code and JetBrains, every edit shows up as a diff you can review, modify, or revert. All changes are tracked with checkpoints, so you can easily undo the agent's work. Runs Bash Commands Cline executes commands directly in your terminal and watches the output in real time. Install packages, run build scripts, execute tests, deploy applications, manage databases. For long-running processes like dev servers, Cline continues working in the background and reacts to new output as it appears, catching compile errors, test failures, and server crashes as they happen. Plan and Act Toggle between Plan mode and Act mode. In Plan mode, Cline explores your codebase, asks clarifying questions, and lays out a strategy. Once you're aligned, switch to Act mode and Cline executes the plan. Every file edit and terminal command requires your approval, so you stay in control of what actually changes. Or toggle auto-approve and let Cline run autonomously. Rules and Skills Define project-specific rules in .clinerules files that guide how Cline works in your codebase: coding standards, architecture conventions, deployment procedures, testing requirements. Rules are picked up automatically by the CLI, VS Code extension, and JetBrains plugin. Use skills to let the model load specific rules when needed. Works With Every Model Cline is not locked to a single AI provider. Use whichever model fits your workflow: Provider Models Anthropic Claude Opus, Sonnet, Haiku OpenAI GPT series models Google Gemini series models OpenRouter 200+ models from any provider Vercel AI Gateway Route to many providers through one gateway AWS Bedrock Claude, Llama, and more Azure / GCP Vertex All hosted models Cerebras / Groq Fast inference models Ollama / LM Studio Run local models on your machine Any OpenAI-compatible API Self-hosted or third-party endpoints Extend With Plugins or MCP Servers Extend Cline's capabilities with plugins. Using the SDK, register tools and lifecycle hooks programmatically through the plugin system for logging, auditing, policy enforcement, or adding domain-specific capabilities. Simple plugin example below. import { Agent , createTool } from "@cline/sdk" const deployTool = createTool ( { name : "deploy" , description : "Deploy the current branch to staging." , inputSchema : { type : "object" , properties : { env : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "env" ] } , execute : async ( input ) => { // your deployment logic } , } ) const agent = new Agent ( { tools : [ deployTool ] , /* ... */ } ) ...or use MCPs to connect to databases, query APIs, manage cloud infrastructure, and interact with external systems. Use community-built servers or ask Cline to create custom tools on the fly. In the CLI, manage servers with cline mcp . Multi-Agent Teams Coordinate multiple agents working together on complex tasks. A coordinator agent breaks the work into subtasks and delegates to specialist agents, each with their own tools and context. Team state persists across sessions so you can pick up where you left off. cline --team-name auth-sprint " Plan and implement user authentication with tests " Scheduled Agents Run agents on cron schedules for recurring automations. Daily PR summaries, weekly dependency checks, codebase health reports. Schedules persist across restarts and run independently of any terminal session. cline schedule create " PR summary " \
  --cron " 0 9 * * MON-FRI " \
  --prompt " List all open PRs and their review status " \
  --workspace /path/to/repo Connect to Slack, Telegram, Discord, and More Chat with your agent from any messaging platform: Telegram, Slack, Discord, Google Chat, WhatsApp, and Linear. Each conversation thread maps to an agent session with full context. Set up access control to restrict who can interact with your agent. # Connect to Telegram cline connect telegram -k $BOT_TOKEN # Connect to Slack through webhook cline connect slack --bot-token $SLACK_TOKEN --signing-secret $SECRET --base-url $URL # Connect to Slack using socket mode cline connect slack --bot-token $SLACK_TOKEN --app-token $SLACK_APP_TOKEN Headless CLI for CI/CD Run Cline with zero interaction for scripting and automation. Pipe input, get JSON output, chain commands, integrate into CI/CD pipelines. cline " Run tests and fix any failures " git diff origin/main | cline " Review these changes for issues " cline --json " List all TODO comments " | jq -r ' select(.type == "agent_event" and .event.text) | .event.text ' Contributing Start with the Contributing Guide . title: mixelpixx/Konnect
abstract:
Konnect *BETA Release AI-assisted PCB design for KiCAD 10. Konnect is a native KiCAD plugin — a single
Rust binary — that lets Claude and other AI assistants design schematics and PCBs
through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). 228 tools across 21 on-demand toolsets. Schematic capture, PCB layout and
routing, ERC/DRC, design-review audits, JLCPCB part search, reference
circuits, and a full manufacturing export pipeline — with bundled skills and agents
that teach Claude KiCAD conventions out of the box. Status: beta. The core toolchain is tested and working, but this is a young
release and it wants real-world mileage and review. Issues and PRs are welcome —
see CONTRIBUTING.md and the naming conventions . Add realtime research to KiCAD MCP and Konnect. Introducing Nimrod Nimrod is our web-research MCP server:
quality-scored Google search, clean webpage extraction, and deep multi-source
research. Design the board with Konnect while Nimrod pulls live parts availability, datasheets,
and errata — no more guessing from year-old training data Works with claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, VS Code, and any MCP client 1 credit = 1 search · extraction always free · free 50-credit trial, no card Official MCP Registry: ai.orchis/nimrod Why Konnect exists Konnect is the successor to KiCAD-MCP-Server ,
a Python/TypeScript project that proved AI-driven PCB design works — and, in the
process, showed exactly where that architecture runs out of road. Konnect was built
to fix those specific problems: The call path was too long. In the original server, a single tool call travels
through TypeScript, schema validation, a spawned Python subprocess, JSON over
stdin/stdout, a command router, and finally SWIG-generated C++ proxy objects before
anything touches your board. That's four language and serialization boundaries, each
with its own failure modes — subprocess lifecycle management, stdout parsing that
filters out warnings KiCAD leaks into the stream, chunked-JSON reassembly. In
Konnect, a tool call is a function call. One process, one language, no plumbing. The dependency surface was enormous. Running the original means carrying Node.js
and its npm tree, Python and its pip packages, wxPython, kicad-skip, and KiCAD's
SWIG bindings — two package ecosystems plus a binding layer, every one of them a
moving target that can break an install. Konnect is a single static binary —
20–25 MB depending on platform, a ~9 MB download. There is nothing to install
alongside it and nothing to version-match. SWIG is a dead end. The original's PCB backend depends on KiCAD's SWIG Python
bindings, which KiCAD is deprecating in favor of its IPC API. SWIG also carried
real operational scars: a zone-fill call that can segfault the backend, proxy-object
comparison bugs, and a fallback path that can silently swap backends mid-session.
Konnect talks to KiCAD 10 through the official IPC API (protobuf over NNG) — the
interface KiCAD is investing in — with real-time board edits that integrate with
KiCAD's own undo/redo. Schematic edits should not corrupt files. Konnect edits .kicad_sch files
through its own S-expression engine with atomic writes (write, fsync, rename), UUID
preservation, and round-trip tests — no third-party schematic library with known
gaps, no text-manipulation workarounds. Context economy is a feature. Exposing all 228 tools to an LLM costs roughly 23K
tokens of context on every listing. Konnect's router loads a starter kit (~2K
tokens) and lets the model pull in toolsets on demand — plus built-in observability
( get_recent_calls , server_stats , JSONL call logs) so the model can diagnose its
own tool failures. The result is smaller, faster to install, aligned with where KiCAD is going, and
built for production use rather than experimentation. The original project remains
open, maintained, and useful — see the comparison below . What it does Instead of describing changes and applying them by hand, the AI works your project
directly: Place and wire schematic components — add resistors, ICs, connectors; wire them
together by pin name Lay out the PCB — place, move, rotate, and route footprints in real time via
KiCAD's IPC API, with full undo/redo integration Run design checks — ERC, DRC, connectivity validation, decoupling audits,
power-rail review, BOM health checks Export production files — Gerbers, drill, BOM, pick-and-place, 3D models, PDF Search JLCPCB parts — find in-stock components in a local 2.5M-part catalog and
suggest alternatives Start from reference circuits — USB-C, LDO, buck converter, STM32, I2C, LED
templates with verified component values Watch it happen — a live schematic viewer auto-refreshes as the AI edits The full tool catalog is documented in tool-directory.md . How it works Layer Mechanism Schematic editing Direct .kicad_sch S-expression editing with atomic writes (no KiCAD required) PCB editing KiCad 10 IPC API (NNG + protobuf) — real-time and undo-aware; single-footprint placement has a safe headless fallback Specctra routing Revision-bound Rust DSN export, local Freerouting MCP routing, and strict one-transaction SES import; an authenticated KiCad 10 native-export bridge is explicit opt-in Exports & checks kicad-cli subprocess (Gerber, PDF, ERC, DRC, …) Transport MCP JSON-RPC over stdio (default), or Streamable HTTP ( transport = "http" / "both" ) Explore the request path and safety boundaries in the interactive architecture diagrams . They are
published from a standalone documentation repository and add no dependencies to
Konnect. Installation From the KiCAD Plugin Manager (recommended) Download the package for your OS from Releases : konnect-pcm-v<version>-windows.zip , -macos.zip , or -linux.zip . Each
bundles that platform's server binary — the macOS package is a universal
build, so one download covers Apple Silicon and Intel. (The konnect-pcm-* assets are the KiCAD plugin packages; the other archives are standalone
server binaries.) Open KiCAD 10 → Plugin and Content Manager Click Install from File and select the zip Restart KiCAD Verify: open the PCB Editor → Tools → External Plugins → you should see Konnect . For KiCad 10, the Konnect settings dialog also offers an optional native
Specctra bridge . When enabled, export_specctra_dsn can ask the active PCB
Editor to generate its native DSN while Konnect still binds the export to the
exact IPC snapshot and creates the strict reverse manifest used during SES
import. The bridge is local-only, authenticated, disabled by default, and not
the KiCad 11 integration path. Konnect uses its Rust exporter by default; native_bridge_mode: "prefer" enables fallback to Rust when the bridge is
unavailable, while "require" refuses instead. For end-to-end autorouting, run check_freerouting , then export_specctra_dsn → route_specctra_dsn → plan_specctra_ses_import / apply_specctra_ses . Readiness reports engine
discovery, native-MCP compatibility, and complete bridge availability
separately. The owned Java child is loopback-only and is reaped on success,
failure, timeout, or cancellation. The first supported profile preserves fixed
straight tracks and through vias; unlocked routing, arcs, zones, and unsupported
geometry are rejected before mutation. Build from source # protoc is required (protobuf code generation), and cmake (the nng crate # compiles the NNG C library with it). # Windows: choco install protoc cmake # macOS:   brew install protobuf cmake # Linux:   apt install protobuf-compiler cmake cargo build --release -p konnect Install guidance for your AI client Konnect bundles shared KiCad skills for Claude and Codex. Select the client when
installing, checking, or removing that guidance: # Existing behavior remains the default: Claude skills, agents, and hooks konnect init # Codex installs only the shared skills under ~/.agents/skills konnect init --client codex
konnect status --client codex
konnect uninstall --client codex MCP server startup never installs or restores guidance.

title: GCWing/OpenBitFun
abstract:
English · 中文 Built to keep going. OpenBitFun is a highly customizable, open-source agent workspace that keeps work moving your way. Four powerful Agent Harness modes · Cross-device remote control · Customization from Mini Apps to source If this is the kind of agent workspace you want, ⭐ Star OpenBitFun and help more people discover it. Download Desktop · Mobile Releases · Mini App Marketplace · Contribute OpenBitFun 1.0.0 is here OpenBitFun 1.0.0 brings a redesigned interface, four Agent Harness modes for different
kinds of work, and major upgrades to cross-device collaboration and remote control, so
tasks move smoothly across desktop, mobile, and browser. Migration note: OpenBitFun 1.0.0 is not data-compatible with legacy 0.2.x releases. To migrate legacy data,
use the OpenBitFun Data Tools , currently available
for stable releases 0.2.17–0.2.19. Four modes for the way you work The Agent Harness shapes how a task gets done. It plans steps, manages context, calls tools, coordinates agents, and brings their results together. Choose the mode that fits the task: Mode When to use it Minimal Quick collaboration. Start with a clear goal. The agent acts directly, you give feedback, and you refine the work together. Standard Everyday tasks. For work with several steps: plan the approach, work through it, and check the results. Ultimate Complex tasks. Dig into demanding problems, divide the work among agents, and bring their results together. Creative Creation and customization. Build Mini Apps or extend OpenBitFun's interface and capabilities to make the workspace your own. Your agent, across devices Switch devices. Keep the task moving. Start at your desktop, pick up the conversation on your phone, or use a browser to check progress, add instructions, and respond to approval requests. Work continues on the device running the task, wherever you connect from. On mobile, switch between layouts for one, two, or three screens. Focus on the conversation with a single screen, then unfold your phone to view conversations and files side by side. The interface adapts as the screen layout changes. We're also building ways to connect from watches and glasses. The device extension protocol lets us bring task updates and simple interactions to more wearables, extending collaboration from your desk to your wrist and beyond. Connection and deployment details Use SSH to work on a remote host, through a jump host, or inside a container, with files, commands, and agent execution in the target environment. The desktop app and CLI share core execution capabilities; mobile clients and messaging bots offer more ways to control tasks. Account login, synchronization, and control between devices on the same account run through a Relay server you deploy . See Remote Connect and remote workspaces for connection options. Turn everyday needs into useful apps Build a Git insights panel for a repository, a workspace for presentations, or a form that brings routine actions together. Mini Apps turn specific needs into tools you can use. Describe what you need and let the agent build it. Each Mini App pairs a dedicated interface with an agent conversation, so you can use the app for everyday work and keep improving it through chat. Install and reuse the apps you build, or explore the Mini App Marketplace for tools that fit your work. Extend OpenBitFun with OpenBitFun Customize the roles, tools, interface, and source code. Start with an agent that fits your work, then extend the workspace around it: Build a specialist agent. Choose a model, define its role, and equip it with the tools and workflows it needs for motion comic production, visual design, code review, or your own field. Connect tools and workflows. title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
abstract:
AI benchmarks have multiplied in recent years, but coverage of economically valuable work remains limited. To measure this, we compiled relevant benchmarks to measure their coverage of American jobs. This Benchmark Map is our first step toward building a comprehensive, continuously updated resource for understanding AI capabilities across the economy. Each tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks. In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts , and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations. Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks . This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do. The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first: Adjusted probability of task coverage Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered. As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do. To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations. To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized: Following work by Wang et al. , we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks. To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al. ’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task. A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab. Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list. We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering). By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal. Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices. The benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al. ), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation. But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts: Adjusted probability of task coverage Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important: Adjusted probability of task coverage O*NET task importance (1–5 rating scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that, controlling for occupation, an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag and a given quintile O*NET importance score is covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Importance quintiles are calculated from O*NET importance scores. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and importance quintiles, with occupation fixed effects. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.

The ARRL Solar Report Just Ahead in Radiosport Upcoming ARRL Conventions and Major Events Florida Hams Provide Communications Support During Hurricane Isaias Amateur radio operators from Florida’s Santa Rosa, Nassau, Lake, Pinellas, and Leon Counties played an important role in supporting emergency communications efforts during and following Hurricane Isaias, helping ensure that critical communication capabilities remained available throughout the storm. In Santa Rosa County, volunteer amateur radio operators staffed the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) and the evacuation shelter at the Milton Community Center. These volunteers provided a communications link between the shelter and the EOC, relaying situational updates and maintaining readiness to support emergency communications should traditional systems become unavailable. Amateur radio operators across the state also supported auxiliary communications efforts, providing additional capabilities to maintain contact with the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee if conventional communication networks experienced disruptions. "While traditional communications systems have become significantly more reliable over the years, amateur radio continues to serve as a dependable auxiliary communications resource," said Arc Thames, W4CPD, Santa Rosa County Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) and Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES) Program Manager. "When disaster strikes, our volunteers are trained, prepared, and ready to step in wherever we're needed. It's another layer of resiliency that helps protect our communities." Thames also serves as the ARRL Northern Florida Section Emergency Coordinator and the Amateur Radio Liaison to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, supporting the coordination of amateur radio and auxiliary communications resources statewide. "During tropical weather events impacting Florida, our Auxiliary Communications team provides volunteer operators to monitor amateur radio communications at the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee," Thames explained. "This ensures that if someone is unable to reach emergency officials through traditional means, we have another way to receive and relay critical information. We always hope we're not needed, but we're glad to be there just in case when all else fails." — Thanks to ARRL Northern Florida SEC Arc Thames, W4CPD, for the above The Santa Rosa County, Florida, emergency operations center was a hub of activity during the response to Hurricane Isaias. [Photo courtesy Arc Thames, W4CPD] eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear Online marketplace eBay has imposed new restrictions on listings of radio transmitting equipment in response to new FCC rules that took effect this week, but responded to ARRL that its new policy will not apply to gear that operates exclusively on amateur radio frequencies . The FCC’s rules are intended to use its equipment authorization program to protect against “national security threats to the communications supply chain” and cover a wide variety of products. In its Third Report and Order issued on July 23, 2026, the Commission makes clear that online marketplaces share in the legal responsibility to assure that unauthorized RF devices are not offered for sale on their platforms. The rules took effect on October 13. Moving forward, equipment subject to FCC authorization must have its FCC ID number submitted to the marketplace and posted with its listing. There are exemptions for posts already online, “small sellers,” and used equipment, but initial messages to sellers from eBay suggested that an FCC ID would be required in order to post a listing for any equipment that transmits RF energy. In response to a request from ARRL for a clarification relating to amateur radio equipment that does not require FCC authorization, an eBay spokesperson provided the following statement: eBay allows the sale of devices capable of operating only on frequencies that the FCC has allocated for use by Amateur Radio Service licensees. As these devices do not require FCC equipment authorization, FCC IDs will not be required for these listings as an amateur licensee may use his or her license to operate such radios. However, two-way VHF/UHF radio equipment capable of operating outside of the amateur frequency bands cannot be imported, advertised, sold, or operated within the United States, including on eBay, without an FCC equipment certification. If eBay inadvertently takes action against listings for devices that don't require FCC IDs and are otherwise authorized, the affected seller should inform eBay and we will assess whether to remove restrictions from the listing. It should be emphasized that the FCC did not change its underlying equipment authorization rules. Amateur radio equipment, except for commercial HF amplifiers, continues to not require FCC authorization. title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
abstract:
I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline. The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04. Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD. To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge. Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism:
Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback": 1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge. 2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk. 3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now. The Support Wall:
I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform. As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable. If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem. Pura vida! R.S.G.
